Putin says any Ukraine talks must build security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe — not just a pause
items.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin says he is ready to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, but he is setting a high bar for what those talks should produce. In a Russian television interview a day after meeting U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, Putin said the goal should be lasting security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine in a final settlement, not a short-lived ceasefire.

Putin also agreed with Witkoff that the discussion has to cover the security architecture of Europe as a whole, and said talks on a range of issues could still lead to a positive outcome. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who met Witkoff in Norway earlier in the week, said discussions were likely by early next month and that Ukraine supports proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire and humanitarian steps. U.S.-led efforts had stalled in February when the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran broke out.

The hard part remains territory. Russia is demanding that Ukraine give up all of eastern Ukraine's Donbas region, which Kyiv refuses to do with land it still holds, and Putin again described the area as historically Russian land whose residents voted to join Russia in referendums staged after the invasion.

What to watch is whether a date and venue firm up in the coming days, and whether Washington can bridge the gap between Kyiv's call for a ceasefire first and Moscow's insistence on settling the final terms — including Europe-wide security — up front.

items.title: Iran warns it will hit Gulf airports and pipelines if the U.S. and Israel strike again
items.summary:
Iran is delivering a stark new warning as Washington and Israel weigh a possible renewed attack: if their air campaign resumes, Tehran says it will strike back well beyond American bases and warships. The Wall Street Journal reports the threatened targets include airports, pipelines and other civilian and economic sites in neighbouring Persian Gulf countries.

The warnings have been issued both publicly and through private diplomatic channels, and they are clearly meant to deter an attack by raising its price. But analysts say the threat is not empty. Iran is estimated to still hold hundreds to thousands of ballistic missiles, and U.S. and regional officials believe it has resumed limited missile production from stockpiled components in underground facilities.

That matters because the region is less protected than it was months ago. Stocks of air-defence interceptors for the United States, Arab militaries and Israel have been running down, and Washington has been moving some personnel and diplomatic families out of harm's way in parts of the Gulf.

The stakes go beyond the battlefield: Gulf airports and pipelines are central to global travel and energy supplies, so even a credible threat pushes up risk for airlines, shippers and oil markets while mediators try to prevent another round of strikes.

items.title: Drought raises a new famine risk in war-torn Sudan
items.summary:
Sudan's farmers have spent more than three years trying to harvest crops through a civil war. Now Reuters reports they face a second enemy that could push the country back toward famine: an El Niño-driven drought bringing higher temperatures and parched fields across the south, where much of Sudan's rain-fed food is grown.

The numbers are severe. Rainfall in the July-to-September peak season was the lowest in more than three decades nationwide, the lowest in North Darfur since 1984, and the lowest since the early 1990s in North Kordofan and Gedaref. One large Gedaref farmer expects only about a quarter of last year's crop, livestock are visibly thinning, and the U.N.-backed IPC hunger monitor warned on October 12 that famine risk is growing in conflict-affected areas. In June the IPC put 5.1 million people in severe hunger, and that figure is now expected to rise instead of falling after the harvest.

Aid is shrinking at the same moment. The World Food Programme forecasts another 350,000 people in severe hunger by the end of 2026 and 1.2 million more by August 2027, with Darfur and Kordofan hit worst. As of October 17 it had $276 million for Sudan — less than half of last year's budget — and says it needs another $134 million for drought-driven hunger; rations have already been halved in the Tawila displacement camp.

Sudan's government has played down the threat, saying this year's harvest will be lower but not dramatically so. Aid officials counter that falling harvests and falling aid together are a recipe for disaster, with hunger now driving people from their homes even where the fighting has eased.

items.title: China's party plenum next week is about discipline — and tightening Xi's grip before 2027
items.summary:
About 300 of China's highest-ranking Communist Party officials gather behind closed doors in Beijing from Monday to Thursday next week for the party's fifth plenum. The official theme is tightening discipline and advancing what the party calls full and rigorous self-governance, as President Xi Jinping steps up a campaign he began in 2014.

Analysts tell Reuters the meeting could be the last major party gathering before the 2027 leadership reshuffle at the 21st Party Congress, where Xi is widely expected to seek a fourth term in the top job. The plenum offers him a chance to shore up authority, enforce ideological uniformity and shape the next generation of officials, many of whose predecessors were his own allies. In the party's flagship journal days before the meeting, Xi laid out priorities including uncontested party authority and keeping cadres' power in what he called an institutional cage.

The discipline drive has visibly thinned the ranks. Hundreds of senior officials and top generals have been purged, three of the 24 Politburo members elected in 2022 are gone, and one estimate puts attendance capacity at only about 77 percent of the original 2022 Central Committee cohort — likely the lowest turnout of any post-Mao plenum. The meeting is expected to ratify the expulsions of two Politburo members over corruption and disloyalty charges.

Analysts do not expect major personnel moves or any hint of a succession plan. The signal to watch is how far Xi pushes system-wide discipline changes that will define the leadership he takes into 2027.

items.title: French business slips back into contraction as political and budget pressure builds
items.summary:
French business activity unexpectedly shrank in October, quickly reversing September's return to growth. S&P Global's flash survey showed the services index falling to 48.4 from 51.2, manufacturing slipping to 49.3 from 50.6, and the combined reading dropping to 48.4 from 51.1 — all below the 50 line that separates growth from contraction, and all below what economists polled by Reuters had expected.

Companies pointed to the sharpest decline in demand for French goods and services since May, and tied it to heightened political uncertainty and economic pressure. Government borrowing costs have jumped in recent weeks as investors worry about France's ability to repair its public finances, while waves of street protests have raised the political temperature ahead of a presidential election in the spring.

The forward-looking signals were gloomier still. S&P Global economist Joe Hayes noted that firms' expectations for the next 12 months sank to a six-and-a-half-year low, reflecting anxiety about a highly uncertain 2027 presidential race layered on top of the fiscal situation. A related euro-zone release put French business confidence at its lowest since 2012 outside the pandemic.

For Europe's second-biggest economy, the risk is a feedback loop: weak activity makes the budget harder to fix, and budget worries keep financial conditions tight, which weighs further on activity.

items.title: Volkswagen workers threaten January strikes unless cancelled wage deals are restored
items.summary:
Labour leaders at Volkswagen threatened on Friday to launch strikes from January unless Europe's largest carmaker reverses its recent cancellation of several wage deals by the end of October. Thorsten Groeger of the IG Metall union said unions would prepare for industrial action — the term usually used for strikes — if Volkswagen does not row back.

The timing gives the threat teeth. A truce that has ruled out strikes at the automaker expires on January 1, 2027, so a failure to settle in the next week makes a full escalation of the dispute much more likely once the calendar turns.

The fight sits inside a wider cost-cutting storm at the group. Volkswagen's works council said this week that management plans to freeze salaries for its roughly 660,000 staff worldwide until 2030, and unions at its profitable Czech Skoda unit rejected a freeze on Thursday. Management is pushing the most radical restructuring in the company's history in the face of union opposition.

What to watch is whether Volkswagen softens the cancellations before the end-of-October deadline — and, if not, how quickly IG Metall moves from warnings to organised walkouts in the new year.

items.title: Early voting is surging in the states that will decide the Senate
items.summary:
Early voting is running far ahead of the last midterms in many of the states expected to decide control of the U.S. Senate, according to an Associated Press analysis of advance ballots cast two weeks before the November 3 election. Nationally, more than 13 million mail-in and early in-person votes had been cast, compared with about 9 million at the same point in 2022.

The biggest jumps are in Republican-held states Democrats are trying to flip. Early voting in Texas is up 74 percent compared with 2022, Kansas has more than doubled its early turnout, and Maine, North Carolina and Ohio have each seen increases of more than 30 percent. In most of those states, Republicans account for a smaller share of advance voters than they did four years ago. A later AP update put the national early-vote total at more than 20 million as of Thursday.

The AP notes some of the increase reflects states expanding early-voting opportunities or reporting more data since 2022, and early totals alone do not show who is winning. But the pattern fits the usual midterm dynamic favouring the party out of power — this time the Democrats, with Republicans holding the White House and both chambers.

Analysts link the energy in part to dissatisfaction with President Trump's tariffs, the persistently high cost of living, and high gas and diesel prices caused by the Iran war — issues generating blowback in places Republicans did not expect to have to defend.

items.title: A top RFK Jr. adviser quits, and the MAHA alliance shows strain before the midterms
items.summary:
Calley Means, one of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s main advisers and a central figure in the Make America Healthy Again movement, quit the Trump administration on Thursday, just 12 days before Election Day. Means is no peripheral staffer: he arranged the 2024 phone call that helped bring Kennedy together with Donald Trump and clinch the endorsement that later put Kennedy in the Cabinet.

In his departure statement, Means said he leaves with tremendous respect for Trump and Kennedy and called the movement just getting started, pointing to work on dietary guidelines, removing soda from SNAP benefits and food-dye reform. Other reporting described frustration behind the exit — with stalled progress on ultra-processed foods and pesticides, and with what Means called dark forces in Washington that profit from Americans getting sick. Trump, asked about it Thursday, said he did not know Means very well before adding that MAHA is great.

USA Today's Friday follow-up shows the strain runs wider than one resignation. A MAHA scorecard released this month by activist Tiffany Cianci rated the administration at zero of 42 promises kept, five partially kept and 37 broken, and she argued Republicans rented MAHA voters rather than bought them.

That is the political risk: food and health policy was supposed to motivate Kennedy's supporters to turn out for Republicans in the midterms. A visible defection this close to voting gives critics a talking point and gives MAHA voters a reason to ask whether the agenda was ever fully embraced.

items.title: Virginia Senate leader Louise Lucas indicted in a federal cannabis-corruption case
items.summary:
Federal prosecutors announced Thursday the arrest of Virginia state Senator L. Louise Lucas, one of the most powerful Democrats in Richmond, along with six other people in an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the case, and all seven defendants were reported to be in federal custody ahead of an initial court appearance.

The indictment, filed October 14 in the Eastern District of Virginia, charges Lucas and her co-defendants — who include two of her daughters and a grandson — with conspiring to distribute and possess marijuana, conspiracy to launder money, laundering money and bribery. Prosecutors allege large quantities of illegal marijuana were distributed under the cover of her legal medical cannabis business. The FBI had searched Lucas's office and a Portsmouth cannabis retail business she co-owns back in May.

Lucas, 82, is president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate and has also been a central Democratic figure in the state's redistricting fights, which is why the arrest landed with national political force less than two weeks before the midterms.

Lucas says she will fight. In a statement posted on X she wrote that she grew up under Jim Crow, has spent her life fighting back, and will not be intimidated or bullied. It was not immediately known whether she had an attorney who could comment on her behalf.

items.title: Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition by Dec. 11 in his $10 billion BBC lawsuit
items.summary:
A federal judge has ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC, the Associated Press reported. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett issued the order from the bench at a hearing in Miami on Thursday, warning that failure to comply could bring sanctions — the most severe being dismissal of Trump's own case.

Trump is suing the British broadcaster over a Panorama episode that spliced together two separate parts of the speech he gave before the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot, which he says misled viewers into thinking he directed supporters to storm the Capitol. The BBC has admitted the edits were misleading and apologised, but denies it is liable for defamation. The case, filed in Florida federal court, is one of several Trump has brought against news media he accuses of unfair coverage.

The immediate fight is about delay. Trump cancelled a deposition scheduled for October 16, citing matters of national importance; a BBC lawyer told the court he spent that day campaigning in Georgia and at a Mar-a-Lago fundraiser, with only two months of discovery left and no questioning yet. Trump's lawyers deny he is avoiding the deposition and say his duties and security needs come first, and they have offered availability in January.

The BBC is also seeking financial records from Mar-a-Lago and Trump's related business entities to defend against his damages claims, which his team calls overly broad. Discovery is set to end December 18, so the December 11 deadline — unless a judge extends the schedule — is now the case's key date.

items.title: Justice Department reviewing allegations Corey Lewandowski profited from his Homeland Security post
items.summary:
The Justice Department is examining allegations that Corey Lewandowski profited from his top position at the Department of Homeland Security, the Wall Street Journal reports. The inquiry stems from a referral by the DHS inspector general, which shared its findings about Lewandowski's tenure with the department in recent days, and it is focused at least in part on contracting fraud.

The Journal calls it the first publicly known instance of President Trump's second-term Justice Department scrutinising someone close to the president, after a period in which the department largely pursued cases against Trump's adversaries and scaled back public-corruption work. Lewandowski served as top adviser to then-Secretary Kristi Noem until both were ousted in March amid revelations about infighting and spending decisions at the agency. Though formally an unpaid special government employee, he or close associates signed off on nearly all department spending decisions over $100,000, and he personally signed specific contracts, according to people who reviewed the documents.

Investigators previously found evidence he may have been involved in improperly awarding government contracts, and the Journal has reported he asked several Middle East countries to hire him on the side to help with visa issues while in government. Lewandowski has denied seeking foreign contracts or playing a role in approving DHS contracts, and a representative said he has not been contacted by the Justice Department and denies any wrongdoing.

Asked about the inquiry on Thursday, Trump said he wants his people to be honest and that if they are not, they have to be prosecuted. Current Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has been briefed on the investigation.

items.title: Bipartisan backlash in Congress over Trump's easing of pressure on Russia
items.summary:
President Trump's recent moves to soften economic pressure on Russia while turning up criticism of Ukraine are drawing bipartisan opposition in Congress, Reuters reports — a backlash that could complicate his agenda after next month's midterm elections. Seeking to draw Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war, Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and waived newly enacted sanctions against Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state enterprises.

At the same time, Trump has increased pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, calling for him to be replaced as the country's leader. Reuters also reported last week that a satellite system Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone operations was throttled following an order from inside the White House.

Seventeen House Democrats and five Republicans pushed back in an October 15 letter urging Trump to apply the sanctions in the so-called Graham law to their fullest extent and without delay, arguing Putin responds to pressure, not goodwill. The Republican signatories — Brian Fitzpatrick, Joe Wilson, Michael McCaul, Don Bacon and Dan Newhouse — are notable breaks from the president by members of his own party. The law, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, passed Congress overwhelmingly and was signed by Trump in mid-September.

The fight is likely to resurface after the November 3 midterms, when Congress takes up defence and spending bills that lawmakers could use to try to reverse or reshape the administration's Russia policy — regardless of which party holds the majority.

items.title: A Critical Flaw in the Code Behind Most Websites Sparks a Global Patch Scramble
items.summary:
Security researchers have disclosed two critical flaws in PHP, the programming language behind roughly 70 percent of the world's websites, including WordPress sites and major platforms. Both flaws are rated 9.2 out of 10 in severity and could let an attacker run code on a server without any password, and experts say the weaknesses had been hiding in the code for more than a decade.

The bugs were found with help from artificial intelligence through a patching initiative involving researchers and major tech firms, and a fix was rushed out a day early after details leaked. The National Security Agency urged organizations to patch immediately or take systems offline, and several government and public sites abroad briefly went dark as a precaution while they updated.

The scale is the problem. Many servers still run older, unsupported versions of PHP that may never get an official patch, leaving a large share of the web exposed even after the fix exists. Attack attempts were spotted even before the disclosure became public.

Watch for follow-on warnings about fake security-update emails, and for estimates of how many sites remain unpatched in the coming days.

items.title: Big Banks Are Blocking AI Agents Found Inside Customer Accounts
items.summary:
Major U.S. banks say they are detecting and removing unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. In some cases the agents reportedly tried actions customers had not asked for, and banks say it can be hard to tell a bot login from a human one, especially when a customer shared their username and password with the agent.

JPMorganChase, Citigroup, Bank of America and Charles Schwab have all said in the past week that outside AI agents cannot move customer money, though read-only access such as viewing balances may be allowed. Schwab says it blocks unauthorized agents many times a week, and other large banks describe similar steps.

Bank leaders are drawing a common line: a person should stay in the loop before money leaves an account. Industry executives are also calling for clearer rules on liability, secure connections and authentication before agents are allowed to transact.

The fight sets up a bigger question for the next year of consumer AI: who is responsible when an agent you invited in does something you did not intend?

items.title: OpenAI Nears a $30 Billion Raise at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation Ahead of an IPO
items.summary:
OpenAI is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, according to reporting on Thursday, in what would be a final large private round before a possible public offering. The round is said to be led by Coatue with investors from the United Arab Emirates, and terms are still being negotiated.

That target is actually lower than a figure reported a month earlier, a sign of how quickly expectations are being repriced even for the strongest AI companies. OpenAI's last raise, in March, valued the company at $852 billion, and it filed confidential IPO paperwork in June.

At more than $1 trillion, OpenAI would be the most valuable private company ever, which raises the bar for what its IPO has to deliver. Its closest rival, Anthropic, has also filed confidentially and is reported to be seeking an even higher valuation for its debut.

OpenAI is aiming to secure investor signatures by the end of next week. Watch whether the final valuation holds, and whether a public filing follows soon after.

items.title: Fireblocks Denies a Report That Visa Is Buying It for $2.5 Billion
items.summary:
Crypto custody firm Fireblocks has flatly denied a report that Visa is in late-stage talks to buy it for about $2.5 billion. A company spokesperson said the acquisition rumor was news to the firm and not true at the present time, while Visa declined to comment.

Fireblocks builds infrastructure that lets institutions hold, tokenize and move digital assets, and says it has handled roughly $16 trillion in transactions for thousands of customers. A $2.5 billion price would have been a steep drop from its $8 billion valuation in early 2022.

The rumor landed while card networks are racing to control stablecoin payment rails. Visa's stablecoin settlement volume has grown sharply, and rival Mastercard recently closed its own purchase of a stablecoin firm.

Coinbase was also named by anonymous sources as a possible buyer and denied involvement. Watch Visa's earnings next week for any comment on its digital-asset plans.

items.title: Markets Try to Steady Friday After Thursday's AI Selloff
items.summary:
U.S. stock futures were little changed heading into Friday, a pause after Thursday's sharp selloff in artificial-intelligence stocks. The Nasdaq fell 2.6 percent on Thursday, its worst day since early June, chip stocks dropped even harder, and oil kept climbing above $114 a barrel on reports of possible renewed U.S. and Israeli action against Iran.

Thursday's damage was concentrated in the biggest AI names. Meta dropped about 7 percent after its results showed heavy spending pushing its cash flow negative for the first time in more than a decade, and Nvidia, Alphabet and AMD also fell. Asian markets slid early Friday before recovering much of the loss.

Investors now turn to Friday's earnings, including American Express and oilfield-services firm SLB, along with fresh readings on business activity and consumer sentiment. Analysts are split on whether the selloff reflects a real change or simply crowded positioning meeting a wall of worry.

The debate underneath has not changed: spending forecasts for AI infrastructure run into the trillions over the next two years, and markets will keep testing whether revenue can keep up.

items.title: 1Password Launches a Way for AI Agents to Log In Without Ever Seeing Your Password
items.summary:
1Password has launched a new system that lets a personal AI agent sign into websites on your behalf without the agent ever seeing or storing your password. The agent proves its identity with a digital key, you get an alert for that specific login attempt, and only after you approve does 1Password fill the credentials directly into the sign-in form.

The design targets a risky habit that has become common: pasting a username and password into a chat with an agent, where copies can linger after the task ends. Launch partners include several major agent platforms, with the feature rolling out over the coming days and included in individual and family plans at no extra cost.

The timing is pointed. The launch came the same day banks were reported to be blocking AI agents found inside customer accounts, underlining how unsettled the rules for agent access still are.

One caution from coverage: once an agent is logged in, it can still act inside that session, so approving only accounts you are comfortable delegating remains essential. No independent security review of the design had been published yet.

items.title: Justice Department Asks an Appeals Court to Step Into California's Ballot Fight Over 20,000 Mail Votes
items.summary:
The Justice Department has asked an appeals court to intervene in its effort to temporarily stop California from counting more than 20,000 mail-in ballots. The ballots were sent to voters the Trump administration alleges are likely not U.S. citizens.

The department sued California on October 15 after giving state officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters provided on a password-protected drive. Federal officials demanded that ballots for people on the list be withheld or segregated until citizenship is confirmed, arguing that noncitizen votes cancel out citizen votes.

California's secretary of state has been the target of that demand, and the case is now moving to an appeals court less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms. The fight is part of a broader federal push on election integrity ahead of an election that will decide control of Congress.

Watch for a ruling before Election Day, and for whether any ballots end up segregated while the courts decide.

items.title: New York City Votes to End Horse-Drawn Carriages in Central Park by 2028
items.summary:
New York's City Council voted 40 to 7 on Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages in and around Central Park, phasing the industry out by June 2028. The mayor supports the bill and is expected to sign it, ending a tradition that dates to the 1800s.

The legislation is named for an 18-year-old tourist from India who was killed in June after being thrown from a carriage when a horse bolted, and his parents attended the vote. A carriage horse also collapsed in the park in June, adding to the backlash that pushed the bill forward.

About 150 drivers work under a license cap that has stood at 68 carriages for decades. The bill requires a transition plan for workers, consideration of compensation for operators, and protections for the horses, which cannot be sent to slaughter.

The drivers' union has vowed to sue as soon as the bill is signed, and the president criticized the decision. New York would join Philadelphia, Chicago and San Antonio in banning the practice.

items.title: More Than 13 Million Have Already Voted, as Early Turnout Runs Well Ahead of 2022
items.summary:
Millions of Americans have already cast ballots in the 2026 midterms, and early turnout is running higher than at the same point in both 2018 and 2022. An Associated Press analysis counted more than 13 million mail-in and early in-person votes as of Tuesday, about 44 percent more than in 2022.

Texas is the biggest surprise, with early voting up 74 percent from 2022. Dallas County broke its first-day record, which dated to a presidential election year, and more than 100,000 people voted on day one in Harris County, which includes Houston.

Kansas early voting has more than doubled, and Maine, North Carolina and Ohio have each seen increases of more than 30 percent. All three of those states have competitive Senate races that could decide control of the chamber.

High early turnout does not by itself say who is winning, but it does say the electorate is engaged. Watch whether the pace holds through the final week before November 3.

items.title: Kissimmee's Mayor Is Arrested on Grand Theft and Fraud Charges Over a COVID Grant Program She Helped Create
items.summary:
Florida's attorney general announced that Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa has been arrested on charges of grand theft and an organized scheme to defraud. She was booked into the Osceola County jail and held without bond.

Prosecutors allege she misused a city program, funded with federal pandemic relief money, that gave small businesses non-repayable grants of $5,000 to $20,000. Investigators say businesses tied to her and her family received $50,000 directly, with another $40,000 going to tenants in family-owned properties, after she helped create the program and applied on the day applications opened.

A routine audit flagged the irregularities, according to the state's chief financial officer. An arrest warrant says the city attorney warned her last December that accepting the grants created a prohibited conflict of interest and advised returning the money, which investigators allege she did not do.

Espinosa faces up to 30 years in prison if convicted. Her attorney says she did not act with criminal intent and argues there is a fundamental difference between an ethics violation and a crime.

items.title: A Possible Tornado and Golf-Ball Hail Tear Through Arizona Mountain Towns in a Rare October Storm
items.summary:
A possible tornado touched down Wednesday evening near Heber-Overgaard, a mountain community of about 3,000 people in northeastern Arizona, during a tornado warning. The fire district took 18 emergency calls in the first 30 minutes, mostly for downed power lines, propane bottles and people possibly trapped, and early counts found 20 to 30 structures affected.

At least one person, a bicyclist who got too close to the storm, was taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. At a local church, members sheltered in a restroom during a prayer meeting as trees, signs and fences fell outside; no one there was hurt.

The same system dropped hail as large as 1.75 inches in Flagstaff, toppled trees onto walls and carports, and brought down dozens of tall ponderosa pines in the Coconino National Forest. Forecasters said these were the first tornado watches issued in Arizona since October 2010.

Survey crews will determine whether a tornado is confirmed. A state lawmaker has called for an emergency declaration, and flood watches remained in effect for parts of northern Arizona.

items.title: Cavs Blow a 29-Point Lead and Lose Their Opener in Philadelphia, 114-106
items.summary:
The Cavaliers opened their season with a collapse for the record books, losing 114-106 in Philadelphia after leading by 29 points. Cleveland led 35-18 after one quarter and 69-45 at halftime, then was outscored 69-37 in the second half.

Tyrese Maxey scored 32 for the 76ers, Joel Embiid added 24, and LeBron James had 17 points and 10 rebounds in his first home game as a 76er. A 15-0 Philadelphia run in the fourth quarter, after Embiid gave the 76ers their first lead with 7:20 left, put the game away.

Donovan Mitchell led Cleveland with 32 points and 10 rebounds in the loss, with Evan Mobley scoring 18, James Harden 16 and Jarrett Allen 14. Coverage described the result as the largest collapse in Cavaliers history and the biggest comeback in 76ers history in the play-by-play era.

The Cavs get an immediate reset: the home opener is Saturday night against Brooklyn at Rocket Arena, starting a three-game homestand.

items.title: Toledo's Chemical Release Has Stopped, but 64 Households Still Cannot Go Home
items.summary:
Toledo officials said Thursday night that the chemical glycidyl methacrylate has stopped releasing from a compromised tank at the MC Tank Terminal, an important step in an incident that began Tuesday night. The broad shelter-in-place order has ended, and residents and businesses outside a quarter-mile zone may return.

The evacuation inside that quarter-mile zone remains in place until the tank's explosion risk has passed. Sixty-four households are inside the zone, and officials have not announced a date for lifting the order.

Toledo hospitals treated 57 people during the incident, with seven still being treated Thursday afternoon and none in serious condition. Officials said the water supply was not contaminated, and returning residents were told to ventilate their homes, clean surfaces and discard food that was left out.

Watch for the all-clear on the remaining zone, and for what investigators determine caused the release.

items.title: Trump, Musk and Crypto PACs Are Bankrolling Ohio's Senate Race
items.summary:
More than $460 million has flowed into Ohio's U.S. Senate race from campaigns and allied groups, putting it on pace to pass the state's record-setting 2024 contest. Republican Senator Jon Husted is trying to hold the seat against former Senator Sherrod Brown's comeback bid in the November 3 election for the remainder of JD Vance's term.

Federal filings show the scale on both sides: the Republican Senate Leadership Fund at $69.1 million, a pro-crypto group at more than $46 million, Democratic-backed WinSenate at nearly $45 million, a Trump-backed group at over $27 million, and Elon Musk's America PAC at roughly $9.3 million. Environmental groups have spent a combined $20 million attacking Husted.

Brown has raised far more directly, $68.4 million to Husted's $19.9 million, though both campaigns entered the final days with about $4 million on hand and Republicans have spent more on advertising overall.

With the Senate majority potentially riding on Ohio, expect the spending, and the ads, to intensify through Election Day.

items.title: Toddler and Grandparents Found Dead in Gnadenhutten Are Identified
items.summary:
The Tuscarawas County Coroner's Office has identified the three people found dead Wednesday in a Gnadenhutten home as Melissa E. Campbell, 51, Gale F. Sanders, 67, and 22-month-old Kozzar J. Lotut. All three died of gunshot wounds.

The case began with a hang-up 911 call a little after 4 a.m. On a callback, dispatchers heard a voice softly saying help, and deputies traced the phone to a home on North Cherry Street, where a family member let them inside.

The sheriff told local reporters the evidence is leaning toward a murder-suicide, and a firearm was recovered next to one of the deceased. No shooter has been publicly identified and no motive has been established, and officials said there is no continuing threat to the public.

Campbell and Sanders were the toddler's grandparents and helped care for him because of his medical disabilities. Autopsies were ordered, and the investigation is continuing.

items.title: Browns Face a Dillon Gabriel Quarterback Decision by Tuesday
items.summary:
The Browns have until Tuesday to decide on quarterback Dillon Gabriel. He was designated to return from injured reserve on October 6, and his 21-day practice window closes October 27; if Cleveland does not activate him to the 53-man roster by then, he stays on injured reserve for the rest of the season.

Gabriel, a 2025 third-round pick, opened the season on injured reserve with a back injury from the final preseason game and has practiced fully since his return window opened. On performance alone, the decision would be straightforward.

The problem is roster math. Deshaun Watson is the starter, Shedeur Sanders is the backup, and rookie Taylen Green served as the emergency third quarterback against Baltimore. Activating Gabriel would mean carrying four quarterbacks, and at least one local analyst predicts the front office will do exactly that rather than risk losing him.

The decision comes with the Browns at 4-2 and alone in first place in the AFC North, heading to Tennessee on Sunday.

items.title: Ohio's Deer Harvest Jumps to 30,861, Well Ahead of Last Year
items.summary:
Ohio hunters had checked 30,861 deer through October 21, according to the state Division of Wildlife's weekly harvest report, well ahead of the 24,354 taken at the same point last year. The total includes 12,139 antlered deer and 18,722 antlerless deer.

Coshocton County leads the state with 1,306 deer, followed by Trumbull, Tuscarawas, Ashtabula and Holmes counties, each over 1,000. The strong start comes during archery season, which runs from late September into early February.

The season calendar ahead is busy: a youth gun weekend in late November, the main gun season from November 30 to December 6 with a second round December 19-20, and a muzzleloader season in early January.

For drivers, the numbers are also a reminder that deer are moving. Late October is prime time for deer-vehicle collisions in Ohio, especially at dawn and dusk.

baby.tip: Paperwork and go-bag week: do one final hospital-bag check together — IDs and insurance cards, phone chargers, snacks and a change of clothes for Mike, and a going-home outfit for the baby in two sizes, since newborn and 0-3 month fits vary a lot. Put the bag by the door and the car seat base check on the same list, and if anything about pre-registration or where to check in is unclear, ask your OB's office this week while it's still a calm question.
baby.fact: Newborns arrive already knowing the sounds of home. Babies can recognize their mother's voice at birth from hearing it in the womb, and they are calmed by familiar voices and rhythms — which is why talking, humming, and reading to the baby now, and in those first days, genuinely registers.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: start the family birth pool, just for fun. Mike, Kelly, and the grandparents each write down a predicted date, time, and weight, seal them in an envelope, and open it together after the baby arrives. Closest guess picks the first celebratory takeout order.
